newsitem.title: USA: Poland says arms sales date to old contracts.
newsitem.headline: Poland says arms sales date to old contracts.

text.p: Poland played down a newspaper report on Wednesday that it was involved in arms sales to Iran, and U.S. officials said they were confident Poland would not make any more arms deals with the country America considers a sponsor of terrorism.

The Washington Times cited a classified CIA document as saying several prospective members of NATO, including Poland, were involved in arms deals with Iran, Sudan, North Korea and Iraq, all countries identified by the United States as sponsors of terrorism.
Poland made five shipments to Iran of T-72 tanks, equipment and trainers, with the latest delivery taking place last summer, the newspaper said.
The Polish embassy in Washington released a statement indicating that any such shipments were to fulfil old contracts.

"After 1993, Poland has not signed any new contracts with Iran for supply of military equipment. All contacts in this area have been in fulfilment of earlier commitments and in accordance with Poland's international obligations," the embassy statement said.

State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said that in 1995 Poland pledged to cease arms sales to Iran and phase out existing obligations, and "the Polish government has had a very good track record ... in carrying out this commitment."
"We are confident that the Polish government will continue to ensure the full implementation of its commitment," Davies said.

Another U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity said the shipments reported in the Times were "the dribbles of an old contract, a contract that was not a secret" and indicated this was not an obstacle to Poland's prospective NATO membership.
A summit in Madrid in July is set to invite several of Moscow's ex-Warsaw Pact allies -- led by Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to join NATO.

Expansion of NATO has become a major focus of President Bill Clinton's foreign policy, despite Russian opposition. New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has sought to quicken the pace of the alliance's expansion during her current trip to Europe.

The Washington Times article also said a company in Slovenia, a republic in the former Yugoslavia which is also considered a potential NATO member, participated in a deal to supply tank parts to Iran, but was stopped after U.S. protests.

Another former Warsaw Pact ally, Bulgaria, sold some production equipment for a weapons factory to Sudan and is suspected of trying to ship MiG warplane parts to Iraq, the report said. It said another Bulgarian company sold 15 metric tons of explosives to North Korea.

But the State Department said it had enjoyed "excellent cooperation" with most of the European countries named in the article, all ex-communist nations, in closing down the arms trade they formerly carried on with what Washington calls "rogue states".
Davies said Washington was "very pleased with the high level of cooperation" with Slovenia in stopping arms shipments to Iran.

He said the United States had spoken to Bulgaria about its concerns over arms-related transfers to states sponsoring terrorism and had received "excellent cooperation from the Bulgarian government in bringing such sales to a close."
